One primary concept each, checked for duplicated required ANSWERS and not just for duplicated labels. Q1 what each labelled part of an influenza virion is for · Q2 the influenza cycle end to end, plus how mutation makes new strains · Q3 HIV, from why it is a retrovirus to what each of its enzymes does · Q4 the two cycles held side by side and counted · Q5 how an enveloped virus gets out, and what stops it · Q6 antigenic shift, and the strain count that is not optional · Q7 antigenic drift, from a missing exonuclease to a failed vaccine · Q8 four unfamiliar cases answered with machinery from other Books. Two pairs were checked closely and kept apart. Q1(a) explains what the influenza genome is for, while Q2 runs the genome through the cycle in order, and neither answer is the other. Q7(a) credits the missing proofreading exonuclease as the reason mutations arise, while Q7(b) rejects that same phrase by name because that stem makes the genome the subject and the polymerase is not a feature of the genome; the two parts exist to be held apart, and the schemes say so.

Nothing from Books 5 to 9, and nothing from Cluster 3. Antibodies, memory cells, vaccines and immunity are Extension Topic A and appear here only as the consequence of a changed antigen, never as the substance of an answer. Bacterial genetics is Cluster 3. Where the phage appears it is only as the other exit route, at the level of lysis against budding.

Question 1 [9 marks]

Fig. 1.1 shows the main structural features of the influenza virus.

(a) Explain the role of E and F in the influenza virus. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain the role of E and F in the influenza virus. [4]

1. E is neuraminidase.

2. Neuraminidase facilitates the release of newly formed virus from the infected host cell by cleaving the sialic acid receptors.

3. F is single-stranded negative-sense RNA.

4. Maximum one from the following. F comprises the genes for viral proteins, giving at least one example such as RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

5. Or, F is the template for the synthesis of complementary positive-sense RNA, which are used for translation by host cell ribosomes into viral proteins in the cytoplasm, and are templates for making new copies of the single-stranded negative-sense RNA genome in the nucleus.

(b) Describe the role of the HA protein labelled in Fig. 1.1 in the viral reproductive cycle. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Describe the role of the HA protein labelled in Fig. 1.1 in the viral reproductive cycle. [2]

1. HA protein is haemagglutinin, which binds to specific sialic acid receptors on the cell surface of the epithelial cells lining the respiratory tract.

2. It allows the virus to be taken into cells via receptor-mediated endocytosis.

3. A related scheme awards Haemagglutinin and Neuraminidase in full and prints (Reject: HA, NA), so on any part that says state or name, write both words out.

(c) State the location of viral genome replication in the cell. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) State the location of viral genome replication in the cell. [1]

1. The viral genome is replicated in the nucleus.

(d) Fig. 1.2 shows cross-sections of influenza A virus and influenza C virus side by side. With reference to Fig. 1.2, contrast the structure of influenza A virus with that of influenza C virus. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) With reference to Fig. 1.2, contrast the structure of influenza A virus with that of influenza C virus. [2]

1. Must contrast point to point.

2. Influenza A virus has 8 RNA segments whereas influenza C has only 7 RNA segments.

3. Influenza A virus has HA and NA viral proteins on its viral envelope whereas influenza C virus has HEF viral protein on its viral envelope instead. Reject "cell surface membrane" for the envelope.

4. Influenza A virus has a PA subunit on its RNA polymerase whereas influenza C virus has a P3 subunit on its RNA polymerase.

5. Influenza A has RNA segments coding for HA and NA and PA while influenza C has RNA segments coding for HEF and P3.

Question 2 [13 marks]

(a) Describe the reproductive cycle of the influenza virus and explain how new strains of the virus may arise as a result of mutation. [13]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Describe the reproductive cycle of the influenza virus and explain how new strains of the virus may arise as a result of mutation. [13]

Adsorption

1. The haemagglutinin glycoproteins on the viral envelope recognise and bind to sialic-acid containing receptors on the host cell plasma membrane.

Penetration and uncoating

2. The influenza virus enters the host cell by receptor-mediated endocytosis,

3. whereby the host cell membrane invaginates and pinches off, engulfing the virus in an endocytic vesicle.

4. Acidification causes the viral envelope to fuse with the endocytic vesicle membrane,

5. releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm of the cell.

6. The capsid is then degraded by cellular enzymes, releasing the viral nucleic acid.

Replication

7. The viral genome functions as the template for synthesis of a complementary RNA strand,

8. using the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and host RNA nucleotides in the nucleus.

9. This complementary RNA acts as a template for the synthesis of new copies of viral RNA, that is the genome,

10. and functions as mRNA which undergoes translation to produce viral proteins, for example capsid proteins and glycoproteins for the viral envelope.

Maturation

11. The glycoproteins synthesised by ribosomes on the ER are transported to the host cell's plasma membrane via vesicles and incorporated into the plasma membrane.

12. The capsid is assembled around the viral RNA genome and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

Release

13. The new influenza viruses bud off from the host cell's plasma membrane, so the new viruses acquire their lipid bilayer from the plasma membrane of the host cell, with viral proteins and glycoproteins embedded.

14. Neuraminidase catalyses the cleavage of sialic acid residues from haemagglutinin, facilitating the release of the newly replicated viruses for the next round of infection.

15. Maximum 11 marks for points 1 to 14.

Antigenic drift

16. Point mutations in the haemagglutinin gene in influenza virus occur during the replication of viral RNA.

17. Accumulation of mutations results in slight changes to the shape of haemagglutinin,

18. leading to antigenic drift.

19. The shape of the new haemagglutinin is now complementary to other membrane receptors found on new types of host cells.

20. Quality of written communication: good spread of knowledge communicated without ambiguity, to include at least 1 marking point from each of the 2 sections, the reproductive cycle of the virus in points 1 to 14 and antigenic drift in points 16 to 19.

21. Two corrections to hold while you write this. Your chapter 4.1 page 27 says the endocytic vesicle fuses with an acidic lysosome. It does not: the endosome itself becomes acidified, and fusion with a lysosome would deliver the virion to hydrolases and destroy it. And the correct cause of the mutation rate is that the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase has no proofreading exonuclease activity of its own, not that the host lacks proofreading, which page 36 wrongly says.

Sources & concepts

Source: JJC Prelim 2017 P3 Section B Q4(a), a free-response essay, stem, key and quality of written communication line verbatim, at its real 13 marks. Marking point 21 is added from the digest of the school's own chapter and from the mark schemes that credit the polymerase explanation, and is flagged as an addition rather than part of the JJC key. Archetype: the full-cycle process question, and the single most rehearsed object in Book 4. Book 4 essays are process-led: almost every one of the 22 essay-scale in-scope stems asks for a process in order plus one rider. This is the influenza process plus the mutation rider. Trap: giving fusion with a lysosome instead of acidification of the endosome, which is what your own notes say and is wrong; forgetting that the positive-sense copy does two separate jobs and losing one of the two marks; saying the virus leaves by exocytosis, which a scheme rejects for an enveloped virus that takes the cell surface membrane on its way out; running the whole 13 marks on the cycle and giving nothing on drift, when the quality of written communication mark requires at least one point from each section; describing the mutation rate as caused by the host. LOs: 2(e)ii the reproductive cycle of enveloped viruses including influenza, in full; 2(f) how variation in viral genomes arises, specifically antigenic drift. Concepts fused: (1) haemagglutinin binding sialic acid; (2) receptor-mediated endocytosis; (3) membrane invagination and vesicle formation; (4) acidification triggering fusion; (5) nucleocapsid release; (6) uncoating; (7) negative-sense template; (8) the viral replicase and where it works; (9) the positive-sense copy as a genome template; (10) the positive-sense copy as mRNA; (11) glycoprotein routing through the ER, Golgi and vesicles; (12) assembly around the genome and the enzyme; (13) budding as the acquisition of the envelope; (14) neuraminidase freeing the virion; (15) point mutation during replication; (16) accumulation as the mechanism of drift; (17) altered conformation as the consequence; (18) altered host range as a further consequence.

Question 3 [11 marks]

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a retrovirus and has two main types, HIV-1 and HIV-2. Fig. 3.1 shows the structure of HIV.

(a) Explain why HIV is called a retrovirus. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain why HIV is called a retrovirus. [2]

1. HIV is an RNA virus, that is it has an RNA genome.

2. It needs to undergo reverse transcription to obtain a DNA intermediate to be used for transcription to produce viral RNA and mRNA which is translated to produce viral proteins.

3. The examiner's note on this key is that some students were mistaken and wrote that HIV has negative-sense RNA; they only need to state that HIV's genome is RNA in nature.

4. Two other schools set the same question and are stricter, so write the strict version, which scores under all three. TMJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q1(d): HIV carries single-stranded positive-sense RNA as its genetic material, with "HIV has RNA" alone rejected; during its reproductive cycle, HIV uses its single-stranded RNA as a template and it is reverse transcribed to form single-stranded DNA, then into double-stranded DNA, by reverse transcriptase; the double-stranded DNA then integrates into the host's DNA or chromosome as a provirus.

(b) Describe how an enveloped virus such as HIV enters a host cell. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Describe how an enveloped virus such as HIV enters a host cell. [4]

1. gp120 on the surface of the HIV binds to the CD4 receptor expressed on T-helper cells and/or macrophages.

2. gp120 then undergoes a conformational change to bind to co-receptor CXCR4 on T-helper cells, or CCR5 on macrophages.

3. gp41 then pulls the virus closer to the host cell.

4. The HIV envelope then fuses with the host cell membrane, to release viral contents into the host cell.

5. Misconceptions recorded on this key: referring to gp120 and gp41 as receptors instead of glycoproteins; stating that CD4 undergoes the conformational change instead of gp120; writing gp40 for gp41; describing entry via receptor-mediated endocytosis instead of membrane fusion. As the command word is describe and the question names HIV, vague answers such as "proteins on the viral envelope bind to receptors on host cells" earned no marks.

(c) With reference to Fig. 3.1, describe how the enzymes shown in the diagram are involved in HIV infection. [5]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) With reference to Fig. 3.1, describe how the enzymes shown in the diagram are involved in HIV infection. [5]

1. Reference to reverse transcriptase.

2. The idea of formation of viral DNA. Reject the idea that RNA is turned into or converted into DNA.

3. From viral RNA.

4. Reference to integrase.

5. The idea of integration of viral DNA into host DNA. Accept the idea of latency or of formation of a provirus.

6. The idea that T helper cells would be destroyed, killed or burst by virus particles leaving the cell.

7. The idea that more T helper cells would become infected.

8. Quality of written communication is credited, focusing on clarity of expression.

Question 4 [7 marks]

(a) Some features of the reproductive cycle of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are listed. How many of these features also occur in the reproductive cycle of the influenza virus? [1]

  • penetration
  • integration with host DNA
  • formation of cDNA
  • transcription of viral DNA
  • assembly of new virus particles
A2
B3
C4
D5
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) How many of these features also occur in the reproductive cycle of the influenza virus? [1]

1. The key is A, two.

(b) Explain your answer, saying for each of the five listed features whether it also occurs in the reproductive cycle of the influenza virus, and why. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain your answer, saying for each of the five listed features whether it also occurs in the reproductive cycle of the influenza virus. [4] [INFERRED: the 9477 specimen papers ship without a mark scheme; the per-feature reasoning is cross-checked against NYJC Prelim 2022 P2 Q5(d) and MI Prelim 2018 P2 Q2(b), whose keys contrast the two cycles on the same axes]

1. Penetration occurs in both. Both viruses enter a host cell, though by different routes: influenza by receptor-mediated endocytosis followed by fusion with the endosome membrane, HIV by fusion of its envelope with the host cell surface membrane at the surface.

2. Integration with host DNA does not occur in influenza. Influenza never makes DNA and its genome is never integrated; integration is done by HIV integrase and produces the provirus.

3. Formation of cDNA does not occur in influenza. Influenza carries no reverse transcriptase, so no DNA intermediate is made at any point in its cycle.

4. Transcription of viral DNA does not occur in influenza. There is no viral DNA in an influenza-infected cell to transcribe; the influenza genome is copied by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, and it is the HIV provirus that is transcribed by host RNA polymerase.

5. Assembly of new virus particles occurs in both. Both viruses package their genome with their associated proteins and enzymes before leaving the cell.

6. So the two shared features are penetration and assembly, which is why the key is A.

(c) Explain why enveloped viruses such as HIV will not exit their host cells the same way as the T4 bacteriophage. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain why enveloped viruses such as HIV will not exit their host cells the same way as the T4 bacteriophage. [2]

1. Enveloped viruses exit host cells through budding. Reject: exocytosis.

2. So as to obtain their viral envelope from the host cell surface membrane.

3. T4 bacteriophages are not enveloped viruses, hence they exit the host cell through lysis.

Trap: generalising a DNA stage, reverse transcription or integration from HIV to influenza, which is exactly what the specimen is built to catch; giving exocytosis for HIV, which a scheme rejects by name; comparing yes against no rather than point to point, which schemes reject outright, so say where each virus fuses rather than that one fuses and the other does not. LOs: 2(e)ii and 2(e)iii held together, the reproductive cycles of enveloped viruses and of retroviruses, in (a) and (b); 2(e) exit route by virus, in (c). Reach-back to Cluster 1 for phage lysis in (c). Concepts fused: (1) penetration as a shared slot with different mechanisms; (2) integration as retrovirus-only; (3) reverse transcription as retrovirus-only; (4) transcription of viral DNA as retrovirus-only; (5) assembly as a shared slot; (6) budding as the enveloped exit; (7) where the envelope comes from; (8) lysis as the naked-phage exit; (9) why the exit route follows from whether the virus has an envelope.

Question 5 [10 marks]

(a) Fig. 5.1 shows how the H3N2 influenza virus attacks human respiratory epithelial cells inside the nose. In stage 6, new viruses are formed and released as a result of the action of viral enzyme U. Explain how viral enzyme U helps with the release of new influenza viruses. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain how viral enzyme U helps with the release of new influenza viruses. [1]

1. Viral enzyme U is neuraminidase and it cleaves sialic acid receptors away from the surface of the new influenza particles.

(b) In influenza virus, neuraminidase removes parts of the host cell receptors that bind to haemagglutinin. This helps newly-formed viruses to leave host cells. Drugs have been developed to act on neuraminidase. These drugs prevent viruses from leaving host cells. Suggest and explain how these drugs act to prevent viruses leaving cells. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Suggest and explain how these drugs act to prevent viruses leaving cells. [3]

1. Drugs can be inhibitors of neuraminidase. A competitive inhibitor enters and binds to the active site and competes with the substrate for binding at the enzyme's active site. Alternatively a non-competitive inhibitor binds to the allosteric site and the enzyme's 3D conformation is changed such that the conformation of its active site is altered and the substrate can no longer bind to the enzyme's active site.

2. As a separate point, that is another role of the drugs rather than the inhibitor role, drugs may act by breaking down or hydrolysing neuraminidase, or by disrupting the bonds within the secondary and tertiary structures of neuraminidase, resulting in loss of the specific 3D conformation of the enzyme and its active site, so neuraminidase is denatured and the substrate can no longer bind to the enzyme's active site.

3. No or fewer enzyme-substrate complexes are formed.

4. The host cell receptor is still complementary to haemagglutinin and haemagglutinin remains attached to the receptor, so the newly formed virus does not leave the cells.

5. Marking: point 1 or point 2, and point 4, are compulsory.

(c) EBOV acquires its viral envelope using the same process as HIV. Describe how EBOV acquires its viral envelope. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Describe how EBOV acquires its viral envelope. [3]

1. Glycoproteins and other viral proteins are synthesised and

2. transported to the host cell surface membrane in vesicles,

3. to form exit points for new viral particles.

4. The host cell surface membrane surrounds the viral particles.

5. Immature viral particles bud off from the host cell at the exit points,

6. thus acquiring a viral envelope with glycoprotein from the host cell surface membrane.

(d) Viruses make use of certain properties of the cell membrane to facilitate their release from the host cell. Fig. 5.2 is an electron micrograph of the surface of a host cell, showing a virus in the act of budding out of the membrane. Explain clearly how the structure of the cell membrane facilitates this process. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Explain clearly how the structure of the cell membrane facilitates this process. [3]

1. The phospholipid bilayer structure of the cell membrane provides fluidity, that is lateral movement within their own monolayer.

2. The phospholipids are held by weak hydrophobic interactions between the hydrocarbon tails of the phospholipids,

3. allowing the cell surface membrane to change its shape, that is to be pushed outwards, which is budding.

4. There is the idea of allowing viral glycoproteins to be embedded in the cell surface membrane as exit points.

Question 6 [11 marks]

(a) The diagram shows the emergence of new influenza strains, M and N, resulting in antigenic shift in influenza A. Which events lead to antigenic shift? [1]

Name of eventDescription
1gene mutationgene mutations in the viral genomes of strains K and L occurred in the cell resulting in strains M and N
2recombination of viral genomerecombination of strains K and L resulted in new strains M and N
3reassortment of viral genomereassortment of the viral genomes of strains K and L occurred only when both strains infect the same cell
A2
B3
C2 and 3
D1, 2 and 3
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which events lead to antigenic shift? [1]

1. The key is B, event 3 only.

(b) Explain your answer, saying for each of the three named events whether it is what the diagram shows and whether it leads to antigenic shift. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain your answer, saying for each of the three named events whether it is what the diagram shows and whether it leads to antigenic shift. [3] [INFERRED: the DHS Paper 1 mark scheme gives the letter only; reasoning cross-checked against the ACJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q5(b), EJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q1(e) and JPJC Prelim 2022 P1 Q10 keys, which set the same distinction]

1. Event 1, gene mutation, does not lead to antigenic shift. Accumulated point mutations within a single strain are antigenic drift, not shift, and the diagram shows two strains entering one cell rather than one strain accumulating changes.

2. Event 2, recombination, is not what the diagram shows. Recombination is the exchange of genetic information between two genomes so that a single genome ends up carrying sequence from both. The diagram shows whole intact RNA segments from strains K and L being repackaged into new virions, which is not recombination.

3. Event 3, reassortment, is antigenic shift, and the description is the reason. Reassortment requires that both strains infect the same host cell, because the segments have to be present in one cell at packaging. That condition is what makes it shift.

4. The wider point, and the correction to your own notes. Antigenic shift is a sudden change in the antigenicity of a virus owing to reassortment of the segmented virus genome with another genome of a different antigenic type, and two or more viral strains are involved. Chapter 4.1 page 40 lists two modes of inter-species transmission in which a bird strain jumps to humans without undergoing genetic change, and calls them antigenic shift. Under the chapter's own page 38 definition and its own page 43 table, they are not. A jump with no genetic change is direct cross-species transmission of an unchanged strain.

(c) Explain how influenza virus with eight genomic segments can result in a pandemic. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain how influenza virus with eight genomic segments can result in a pandemic. [2]

1. Antigenic shift.

2. When two different strains infect the same host cell.

3. Genetic recombination of RNA segments, that is rearrangement of genes.

4. During viral assembly.

5. Emergence of a novel strain.

6. Maximum 2.

(d) The sub-types of the influenza A virus that infect birds, humans and pigs in one area of the world in recent times are shown in Table 6.1.

time periodbirdshumanspigs

Student Y claimed that "Antigenic shift of influenza virus is happening within humans, by combining H2N2 from older people with H1N1 or H3N2." State whether or not this statement is true. Give a reason for your answer. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) State whether or not Student Y's statement is true. Give a reason for your answer. [3]

1. False.

2. For antigenic shift to happen, different strains of virus need to infect the same host cell in the same organism, not just the same species.

3. The influenza pandemic wave caused by H2N2 did not happen in the same time period as H1N1 or H3N2, which you can read off Table 6.1.

4. Influenza does not integrate its genome and stay dormant in the host cell, so the H2N2 virus did not stay in the same host when H1N1 or H3N2 infected the human host.

(e) Discuss whether influenza C virus can undergo antigenic shift with influenza A virus. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (e)

(e) Discuss whether influenza C virus can undergo antigenic shift with influenza A virus. [2]

1. The command word is discuss whether, so include both sides of the argument. Maximum 2.

2. Yes: influenza A virus is able to undergo antigenic shift with influenza C virus as they can infect the same species host cells, that is human and pig cells.

3. Yes: influenza A virus is able to undergo antigenic shift with influenza C virus as they have RNA segments coding for the same or similar proteins.

4. No: influenza C is unable to undergo antigenic shift with influenza A virus as it has a different number of RNA segments to influenza A, that is 7 against 8.

5. No: influenza C does not have two RNA segments for HA and NA to exchange with influenza A, or influenza A does not have a HEF RNA segment to exchange with influenza C, or they have different RNA segments coding for different proteins, for example HEF against HA and NA.

Sources & concepts

Source: DHS Prelim 2022 P1 Q13 in full, stem, figure, table and options verbatim, key letter from the official DHS answer grid (a); the follow-on wording in (b) is the drill's, with the reasoning cross-checked against the ACJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q5(b), EJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q1(e) and JPJC Prelim 2022 P1 Q10 keys, and marking point 4 added from the digest of the school's own chapter 4.1; RVHS Prelim 2022 P2 Q5(b), stem and key verbatim (c); ASRJC Prelim 2022 P2 Q5(b)(ii), stem, Table 5.1 and key verbatim (d), renumbered Table 6.1, with the paper's tick-box instruction replaced by "state whether or not"; ACJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q5(d), stem, key and the paper's own note on the command word verbatim (e). The Fig. image is the real diagram from the DHS 2022 Paper 1 question paper. Archetype: figure-led MCQ with every option justified, then applied evaluation. Antigenic shift and drift is only 4.4% of the in-scope the papers but is a whole learning outcome with one of the cleanest reproducible answer structures in the syllabus, so the drill weights it above the papers frequency. Trap: the single most dangerous error in Book 4, which is your own chapter's claim on page 40 that shift can occur without genetic change; calling drift genetic drift, which a scheme rejects by name; defining shift and drift by big change against small change rather than by two or more strains against one strain and reassortment against point mutation; accepting Student Y's claim because H2N2, H1N1 and H3N2 all infect humans, when the requirement is the same host cell in the same organism at the same time; answering (e) one-sidedly when the command word is discuss whether. LOs: 2(f) how variation in viral genomes arises, including antigenic shift, in (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e); 2(d) segmentation of the viral genome as the mechanical precondition for reassortment, in (c) and (e). Concepts fused: (1) mutation as the mechanism of drift and not shift; (2) recombination held apart from reassortment; (3) reassortment as repackaging of whole segments; (4) co-infection of one cell as the precondition; (5) segmentation as the mechanical precondition; (6) assembly as the stage at which reassortment happens; (7) a novel combination of surface antigens as the output; (8) no pre-existing immunity as the reason for a pandemic; (9) same host cell against same species; (10) influenza's lack of latency as a reason two strains cannot meet across decades; (11) segment number compatibility between subtypes; (12) matching gene content as a precondition for exchange.

Question 7 [13 marks]

Fig. 7.1 shows the structure of haemagglutinin (HA) of the influenza virus. The numbers in Fig. 7.1 indicate the positions of amino acids that are frequently changed.

(a) Based on your knowledge of the reproductive cycle of influenza, explain why amino acids in HA are frequently changed. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Based on your knowledge of the reproductive cycle of influenza, explain why amino acids in HA are frequently changed. [3] [INFERRED: the NJC answer booklet leaves this part blank; reasoning cross-checked against the NYJC Prelim 2022 P2 Q5(c)(ii) and ACJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q5(b) keys, which answer the same question]

1. During replication the viral genome is copied by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which has no proofreading exonuclease activity, so errors introduced at each round are not corrected.

2. The virus also has a fast, high rate of replication, so mutations accumulate quickly in the gene coding for haemagglutinin.

3. A change in the nucleotide sequence changes the amino acid sequence of haemagglutinin, and the changes that survive are concentrated in the exposed globular head, which is the surface antibodies bind, because a changed head lets the virus escape existing antibodies while a changed stalk or receptor-binding site would stop it working.

4. The related NYJC key adds that the genome is single-stranded RNA with no backup copy to do correction or repair, and that RNA is more reactive due to the 2' OH group. Its compulsory point is that the change must result in a change in nucleotide sequence and thus amino acid sequence of the glycoproteins.

(b) Explain how specific features of the influenza genome allow variation in the viral genome to arise over time. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain how specific features of the influenza genome allow variation in the viral genome to arise over time. [4]

1. Single-stranded negative-sense RNA.

2. RNA is more unstable or reactive than DNA, allowing a higher rate of accumulation of mutations, that is allowing antigenic drift.

3. 8 segments.

4. Segments allow reassortment, that is new combinations of genome segments when 2 or more strains infect the same cell at the same time, which is antigenic shift.

5. R! lack of proofreading ability by RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Read the reject carefully, because it is not a claim that the polymerase proofreads. The question makes the genome the subject, and the polymerase is not a feature of the genome. The same point is credited freely on a question that asks why mutations arise, as in part (a) above.

(c) Student X claimed that "Antigenic drift of influenza human virus such as H3N2 would lead to vaccines that target haemagglutinin glycoprotein being less effective." State whether or not this statement is true. Give a reason for your answer. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) State whether or not Student X's statement is true. Give a reason for your answer. [3]

1. True.

2. Antigenic drift is caused by accumulation of mutations in the haemagglutinin gene, which changes the shape, conformation or configuration of the H1 haemagglutinin glycoprotein.

3. The mutated H1 protein is more complementary in shape to, that is able to better fit or bind to, receptors containing sialic acid found on the surface of human host cells, and is not complementary to the antigen-binding site of antibodies produced by memory plasma cells.

4. The gene evolves under the selection pressure of virus-specific antibody stimulated from the vaccine.

(d) Suggest how a virus such as SARS-CoV can potentially result in outbreak of new viral diseases. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Suggest how a virus such as SARS-CoV can potentially result in outbreak of new viral diseases. [3]

1. Antigenic shift and reassortment of the viral genome with that of a different antigenic type results in the formation of a new strain.

2. There is spread of viruses from one host species to another.

3. Antigenic drift and gradual accumulation of minor mutations results in changes to the genes for the glycoprotein receptors.

4. Existing viruses have a high mutation rate as replication of nucleic acid does not involve proofreading.

5. The factor that contributed to the outbreak is required but is not itself marked.

6. Examiner comment: "the answers either lacked depth or were conceptually flawed; some students even confused this with a bacteriophage. An outbreak is defined as the occurrence of viral infection cases that substantially surpass the usual levels expected in a particular area. Genetic changes alone, that is antigenic shift and antigenic drift, do not lead to outbreaks. It is important to link the genetic changes to contributing factors such as environmental changes, for example deforestation, human behaviour and movement, for example travel and urbanisation, economic and trade practices, for example illegal wildlife trading, and public health measures, for example access to vaccination."

Sources & concepts

Source: NJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q4(d)(i), stem and Fig. 4.2 verbatim (a), renumbered Fig. 7.1, with the answer inferred because the NJC answer booklet prints this part blank; ACJC Prelim 2021 P3 Q1(e), stem and key verbatim including the reject, (b); ASRJC Prelim 2022 P2 Q5(b)(i), stem and key verbatim (c), with the paper's tick-box instruction replaced by "state whether or not"; School (HCI) Prelim 2024 P2 Q4(d), stem, key and the full examiner comment verbatim (d). The Fig. 7.1 image is the real Fig. 4.2 from the NJC 2023 Paper 2 question paper. Archetype: mechanism explain-chain, run from a property of an enzyme all the way to a public-health outcome. This is the chain LO 2(f) is built on and it is worth several marks run in full and one mark stated at the endpoint. Trap: offering the lack of proofreading as a feature of the genome in (b), which that scheme rejects by name while another scheme credits the same words on a question about why mutations arise; saying genetic drift for antigenic drift; giving shift or drift alone as the cause of an outbreak in (d), which the examiner comment calls out directly; stopping the chain at "the antigen changes" instead of running it through altered 3D conformation, antibodies no longer complementary, no recognition and vaccine failure. LOs: 2(f) how variation in viral genomes arises, including antigenic drift, in (a), (b), (c) and (d); 2(d) the structure and organisation of viral genomes, specifically strandedness, sense and segmentation, in (b). Reach-back to Book 2 for mutation and to Book 1 for protein conformation throughout. Concepts fused: (1) no proofreading exonuclease in the viral polymerase; (2) high replication rate; (3) accumulation of point mutations; (4) where on the protein the surviving changes sit and why; (5) single-strandedness and the absence of a backup copy; (6) segmentation as a separate route to variation; (7) the difference between a property of the genome and a property of the enzyme; (8) altered conformation of the surface antigen; (9) antibodies no longer complementary; (10) selection pressure imposed by a vaccine; (11) genetics plus a contributing factor as the requirement for an outbreak.

Question 8 [8 marks]

(a) The 1968 flu pandemic is one of the deadliest pandemics in history, killing approximately 4 million individuals globally. This pandemic was caused by the novel H3N2 influenza virus. With reference to Fig. 5.1, explain why the H3N2 influenza virus is only able to attack human respiratory epithelial cells. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain why the H3N2 influenza virus is only able to attack human respiratory epithelial cells. [1]

1. Haemagglutinin glycoproteins on the viral envelope can only recognise and bind to specific sialic acid receptor proteins on the cell surface membrane of human respiratory epithelial cells.

(b) With reference to Fig. 5.1, suggest a specific identity of process S, and explain why process S is required for translation to occur. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Suggest a specific identity of process S, and explain why process S is required for translation to occur. [2]

1. Process S is the addition of the 5' cap. This allows for the small ribosomal subunit to bind for translation initiation to occur.

2. Or process S is the addition of the 3' poly(A) tail, that is polyadenylation at the 3' end. This protects the complementary RNA from degradation, or facilitates the export and transport of the complementary RNA from the nucleus into the cytoplasm for translation to occur.

3. Or process S is RNA splicing. This allows for the formation of an mRNA molecule with a continuous coding sequence, or allows different mRNAs to form from the same viral RNA allowing different proteins to be formed.

(c) With reference to Fig. 5.1, suggest the identity of host enzyme T, and explain how host enzyme T helps with the translation of the modified complementary RNA strands. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Suggest the identity of host enzyme T, and explain how host enzyme T helps with the translation of the modified complementary RNA strands. [2]

1. Host enzyme T is aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase. It attaches a specific amino acid to the corresponding tRNA.

2. Or host enzyme T is peptidyl transferase. It catalyses the formation of a peptide bond between adjacent amino acids.

(d) Ebola virus (EBOV) is an enveloped virus containing a cylindrical nucleocapsid that encloses an RNA genome and a viral enzyme. Suggest the identity of the enzyme present in the nucleocapsid of EBOV and explain why this enzyme is needed to form new virions. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Suggest the identity of the enzyme present in the nucleocapsid of EBOV and explain why this enzyme is needed to form new virions. [3]

1. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

2. The host cell does not contain an RNA polymerase that can use RNA as a template.

3. To transcribe the viral RNA into viral mRNA,

4. that the host cell ribosome uses for translation,

5. and for replication, that is to make more copies of the viral RNA.
